title: The Secret of Stubitone™
subtitle: A Point-and-Poke 1086 Domesday Audit Across Fareham, Stubbington & The Solent
sourceAttribution: Verified from Great Domesday Book (1086), Hampshire Folios 4–47 / Open Domesday (CC-BY-SA 3.0, Prof. J.J.N. Palmer)

modernPins.headline: SPLASH! Gosport Doesn't Exist in 1086!
modernPins.verdict: Your pin dropped straight into freezing Solent salt-marsh, gorse scrub, and tidal mud! The name 'Gosport' (God's Port) wasn't even coined until the 12th century—only Alverstoke village stood further south-west, while Bennet Luvet is out here in the mud hugging a turnip!

modernPins.headline: SQUELCH! Portsmouth Isn't Founded Yet!
modernPins.verdict: Portsmouth isn't in the 1086 Domesday Book! Portsea Island had tiny scattered farms (like Buckland and Copnor), while the port town of Portsmouth wasn't founded by merchant Jean de Gisors until around 1180—nearly a century later!

modernPins.headline: VANISHED! Swallowed Without a Name!
modernPins.verdict: Lee-on-the-Solent didn't exist at all, and nearby Chark wasn't even given its own line in Domesday—King William's clerks silently bundled its fields inside the royal manor of Titchfield!

modernPins.headline: SURVIVED! Welcome to 1086 'Stubitone'!
modernPins.verdict: Stubbington beat Portsmouth and Gosport into the history books! Recorded on Folio 46v as 'Stubitone' (Old English for 'Tree-Stump Farm'), it has 9 households, 3 ploughlands, and 2 acres of meadow—seized from Saxon Godwin by Norman Sheriff Hugh of Port!

modernPins.headline: BOOM TOWN! 1086 'Ferham' Rules the Creek!
modernPins.verdict: Fareham is one of the largest settlements on the coast—top 20% in all England! With 90 households, 5 spinning watermills on the Wallington River, 41 acres of meadow, 13 woodland pigs, and 10 enslaved workers, it sits at the head of Fareham Creek.

modernPins.headline: ROYAL CAPITAL! King William's Own Manor!
modernPins.verdict: Titchfield ('Ticefelle') is the administrative capital of the entire Hundred on the River Meon—held personally by King William himself, with 33 households and 2 lucrative watermills!

modernPins.headline: ROMAN WALLS & HALL FISHERY! (No Stone Keep Yet!)
modernPins.verdict: Portchester ('Porcestre') stands inside massive 800-year-old Roman shore-fort walls with 20 households and 'a fishery for the hall' under Norman chamberlain William Mauduit—though its famous tall stone castle keep won't be built until the 1120s!

manors.name: Stubbington
manors.specialNote: Saxon Godwin was completely dispossessed; Sheriff Hugh of Port grabbed Stubbington alongside 50+ other Hampshire manors.

manors.name: Fareham
manors.meaning: Fern Homestead at the Tidal Creek
manors.specialNote: 30 hides taxed at 20 'because of the Vikings, since it is on the sea'. Crashed £18 → £10 after Hastings; Bishop demands £20 'but it cannot bear it'.

manors.name: Titchfield
manors.meaning: Open Land of the Young Goats
manors.specialNote: Passed directly from King Edward to King William as a royal demesne estate—never handed out to a private baron.

manors.name: Crofton
manors.lord1086: Bishop Odo of Bayeux & Alfred of Marlborough
manors.specialNote: Saxon Wulfward lost everything; part went to William's ruthless half-brother Odo of Bayeux (imprisoned by William in 1082!).

manors.name: Rowner
manors.specialNote: Value plunged more than half (£3 10s → £1 10s) during the 1066–67 Conquest shock before recovering under royal treasurer William Mauduit.

manors.name: Portchester
manors.specialNote: Three free Englishmen were merged into one Norman manor with 'a fishery for the hall' inside the Roman walls—decades before the great stone keep!

manors.name: Wickham
manors.meaning: Roman Trading Settlement on the Meon
manors.specialNote: Four Saxon brothers wiped out by Sheriff Hugh of Port; value crashed 60% (£10 → £4) after Hastings and still hadn't fully recovered by 1086 (£7).

stubitoneParchment.folioHeader: HANTESCIRE • XXIII. TERRA HVGONIS DE PORT (Great Domesday Book, Folio 46v)

chunks.latin: Hugo de Port ten' de rege STVBITONE.
chunks.english: Hugh of Port holds STUBBINGTON from the King.
chunks.decoderNote: Notice how STVBITONE is highlighted with a red ink stroke so royal tax clerks could spot village names instantly! Old English 'Stubb-tun' meant a farm cleared among tree stumps.

chunks.latin: Godwinus tenuit de rege E. in paragio.
chunks.english: Godwin HELD it freely from King Edward [before 1066].
chunks.decoderNote: One ruthless Latin verb change tells the whole Conquest story: Saxon Godwin HELD it ('tenuit' — past tense, gone!), while Norman Sheriff Hugh HOLDS it now ('tenet').

chunks.latin: Tunc se defd' p' iiij hid'; modo p' una hida.
chunks.english: Back then it paid tax on 4 hides; now on 1 hide.
chunks.decoderNote: When Saxon Godwin owned Stubbington, it paid tax on 4 hides. Once powerful Norman Sheriff Hugh of Port took over, his tax assessment magically dropped to just 1 hide!

chunks.latin: Terra e' iii car'. In d'nio e' i car' & v vill'i & iiij bord' cu' ii car'.
chunks.english: Land for 3 ploughs: 1 plough on the lord's farm, and 5 villagers & 4 smallholders with 2 ploughs.
chunks.decoderNote: 5 'villani' (villagers) + 4 'bordarii' (smallholders) = 9 heads of household. Their wives, children, and elderly parents (~35–40 more Stubbington locals!) were completely left out.

chunks.english: There are 2 acres of prime hay-meadow.
chunks.decoderNote: Hay meadow was gold-dust in 1086 because it kept heavy plough-oxen alive through freezing Hampshire winters—so every single acre got counted.

chunks.latin: Valuit iii lib'; modo similiter; T.R.E. ii lib' & x sol'.
chunks.english: Worth £3 when acquired; £3 now; in 1066 (T.R.E.) £2 and 10 shillings.
chunks.decoderNote: T.R.E. stands for 'Tempore Regis Eduardi' ('In the Time of King Edward' in 1066). King William forced juries to give THREE valuations: 1066, right after the Conquest, and 1086!

recordedTrue: Stubbington ('Stubitone', Folio 46v): 9 households (5 villagers, 4 smallholders), 3 ploughlands, 2 acres of meadow; Saxon Godwin replaced by Norman Sheriff Hugh of Port (£2 10s → £3).
Fareham ('Ferham'): 90 households, 5 watermills, 41 acres meadow, 13 woodland pigs, and 10 enslaved workers ('servi') under Norman Bishop Walkelin.
Fareham's two famous notes: 30 hides taxed at 20 'because of the Vikings, since it is on the sea', and the Bishop demanding £20 'but it cannot bear it' (true output £16).

Titchfield (King William's royal manor, 33 households, 2 mills), Rowner (14 households, crashed £3 10s → £1 10s), Crofton (17 households, part Odo of Bayeux), & Portchester ('a fishery for the hall').
Real 1086 practices: Juries swearing on holy saint relics, peasants legally forced to pay to use their lord's watermill, and shaved-back-of-neck Norman haircuts (depicted on the Bayeux Tapestry).
comedyComposites: Bennet Luvet ('Boggy Bennet'), Sweating Reeve Odo, Fierce Edith of Stubbington, Gyrth, and Sir Guy are historical composite characters created for this game.

Why did we have to invent their first names? Because the 1086 Domesday Book NEVER bothered recording the names of ordinary English peasants, mothers, children, or enslaved workers—only wealthy landowners like Godwin, Coleman, Wulfward, and Hugh of Port!
(Fun bonus fact: 'Luvet / Louvet' really IS an authentic 1086 Domesday surname meaning 'Little Wolf'—Willelmus Luvet held manors directly from King William!)
blindSpots: Portsmouth & Gosport did NOT exist as towns in 1086—both were founded later in the 12th century.
Smaller hamlets like Chark were silently swallowed inside neighbouring Titchfield without being named.
Roughly 75–80% of real people—women, children, and landless poor—went completely unrecorded because Domesday was a royal tax & feudal power register, NOT a modern population census.
Portchester's famous Norman stone keep wasn't built yet in 1086 (only the Roman fort walls and 'a fishery for the hall' stood there until Henry I's reign in the 1120s).
